items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a community of plants and animals interacting with each other and with the non-living environment (climate, soil, water)”.
items.answer: Ecosystem
items.markingKey: Ecosystem: a community of plants and animals interacting with each other and with the non-living environment (climate, soil, water). [1]

items.stem: Explain why rainforest soils are infertile even though the vegetation is very dense.
items.answer: Most nutrients are held in the biomass; heavy rain leaches nutrients down through the soil; dead material decomposes and is taken up again by shallow roots so quickly that few nutrients stay in the soil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark biomass store; 1 mark leaching; 1 mark rapid recycling [3]

items.stem: Describe the structure (layers) of the tropical rainforest.
items.answer: Emergents up to 50 m; a dense canopy at about 30 m; an under-canopy of smaller trees at about 15-20 m; a shrub layer; and a dark forest floor with little vegetation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for every two layers with heights up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a nutrient cycle diagram for a tropical rainforest drawn as three circles: biomass (large), litter (very small) and soil (small). Thick arrows show fast transfers from litter to soil (decomposition) and from soil to biomass (uptake by roots). An arrow from soil labelled “leaching” and an arrow from litter labelled “run-off” are also shown. Explain why the litter store is very small.
items.answer: Hot, wet conditions all year mean decomposers break litter down very quickly, so it does not build up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rapid decomposition; 1 mark climate reason [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.1, a Gersmehl nutrient cycle for the tropical rainforest. The biomass store is much larger than the litter and soil stores. Transfers from litter to soil and from soil to biomass are very large; losses occur by leaching and surface run-off. (a) Name the largest nutrient store. (b) Explain why the transfer from soil to biomass is large.
items.answer: (a) Biomass. (b) Plants grow all year and their dense, shallow roots absorb nutrients as soon as they are released.

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a nutrient cycle diagram for a tropical rainforest drawn as three circles: biomass (large), litter (very small) and soil (small). Thick arrows show fast transfers from litter to soil (decomposition) and from soil to biomass (uptake by roots). An arrow from soil labelled “leaching” and an arrow from litter labelled “run-off” are also shown. (a) Name the largest nutrient store. (b) Describe how the nutrient cycle would change after the forest is cleared for farming.
items.answer: (a) Biomass. (b) Biomass store shrinks; litter input stops; leaching and run-off losses increase so soil store falls; crops remove nutrients when harvested.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: A student writes: “Rainforest soils are very fertile because the forest is so lush.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The soil is thin and leached; nutrients are stored in the vegetation and recycled quickly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 6.1 shows the percentage of nutrients stored in the biomass, litter and soil. Tropical rainforest: biomass 60%, litter 2%, soil ?. A coniferous (taiga) forest: biomass 25%, litter 50%, soil 25%. What percentage is stored in the rainforest soil?

Table 6.1 shows the percentage of nutrients stored in the biomass, litter and soil. Tropical rainforest: biomass 80%, litter 5%, soil ?. A coniferous (taiga) forest: biomass 25%, litter 50%, soil 25%. Compare the rainforest with a coniferous (taiga) forest.
items.answer: The rainforest stores much more in biomass (80% v 25%) and much less in litter (5% v 50%) and soil (15% v 25%).
items.markingKey: 1 mark comparison with data for two stores [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the nutrient cycle is the main reason why tropical rainforests are fragile ecosystems? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: leaching; nutrient stores; transpiration.
items.answer: For: Most nutrients are held in the biomass; once trees are removed, heavy rain leaches the thin soil and fertility collapses within a few years. Against: Interdependence in food webs means removing one species affects many others; the forest also depends on recycling its own rainfall through transpiration. Climate change and fire threaten even untouched forest. Judgement: The nutrient cycle is a key reason, because clearing breaks it so quickly, but interdependence and the water cycle add to the fragility.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a feature of a plant or animal that helps it survive in its environment”.
items.answer: Adaptation
items.markingKey: Adaptation: a feature of a plant or animal that helps it survive in its environment. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which plants are adapted to the high rainfall of the tropical rainforest.
items.answer: Drip-tip leaves shed water quickly so leaves do not rot; waxy leaf surfaces repel water; buttress roots support trees in waterlogged, shallow soils.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each developed adaptation [4]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which desert plants reduce water loss.
items.answer: Small or no leaves (spines) reduce surface area for transpiration; thick waxy cuticle; stomata that open only at night; hairs that trap moist air.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each developed adaptation [4]

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.4. Plant X: a tall tree with buttress roots, drip-tip leaves and thin bark. Plant Y: a cactus with a swollen stem, a waxy coating, spines and a wide, shallow root system. Suggest why plant Y’s roots spread so widely near the surface.
items.answer: Rain is rare and does not soak deeply, so roots must collect water from a large area quickly before it evaporates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rare rain; 1 mark quick absorption [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.4. Plant X: a tall tree with buttress roots, drip-tip leaves and thin bark. Plant Y: a cactus with a swollen stem, a waxy coating, spines and a wide, shallow root system. (a) State which plant grows in a tropical rainforest and which in a hot desert. (b) Suggest why plant Y’s roots spread so widely near the surface.
items.answer: (a) X: tropical rainforest. Y: hot desert. (b) Rain is rare and does not soak deeply, so roots must collect water from a large area quickly before it evaporates.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark rare rain; 1 mark quick absorption [2]

items.stem: “Plants in hot deserts face greater challenges than plants in tropical rainforests.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: light; soils.
items.answer: For: Water shortage, extreme heat and poor soils limit growth; adaptations such as spines, waxy cuticles and dormancy are needed. Against: Rainforest plants face intense competition for light, heavy rain and nutrient-poor leached soils. Both environments need specialised adaptations. Judgement: Each environment has different but equally severe challenges; deserts limit growth more, but rainforests demand fierce competition.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. items.stem: Explain how a camel is adapted to the hot desert.
items.answer: Can drink about 100 litres at once and survive weeks without water; fat stored in the hump; long eyelashes and closing nostrils keep out sand; wide padded feet do not sink in sand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 6.4 describes two plants. Plant X grows to 45 m, has large ridged roots spreading above the ground, smooth thin bark and leaves with pointed tips. Plant Y grows to 3 m, has a thick, swollen ribbed stem covered in a waxy layer, spines instead of leaves, and roots spreading 10 m just below the surface. Suggest why plant Y’s roots spread so widely near the surface.
items.answer: Rain is rare and does not soak deeply, so roots must collect water from a large area quickly before it evaporates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rare rain; 1 mark quick absorption [2]

items.stem: Fig. 6.4 describes two plants. Plant X grows to 45 m, has large ridged roots spreading above the ground, smooth thin bark and leaves with pointed tips. Plant Y grows to 3 m, has a thick, swollen ribbed stem covered in a waxy layer, spines instead of leaves, and roots spreading 10 m just below the surface. (a) State which plant grows in a tropical rainforest and which in a hot desert. (b) Explain how two features help plant X to survive.
items.answer: (a) X: tropical rainforest. Y: hot desert. (b) Buttress roots support the tall tree in shallow soil; drip tips shed heavy rain to stop rot; thin bark because no protection from cold is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 2 marks each developed adaptation [4]

items.stem: Ravi argues that animals in hot deserts are better adapted to their environment than animals in tropical rainforests. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement.
items.answer: For: Desert animals survive extreme heat and little water: camels store fat and tolerate dehydration; fennec foxes lose heat through large ears; many are nocturnal. Against: Rainforest animals are equally specialised: prehensile tails, camouflage (sloths), specialised diets and climbing skills for life in the canopy. Both sets of adaptations suit very different challenges. Judgement: Neither is “better adapted”: each species is adapted to the particular pressures of its own ecosystem.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the permanent clearing of forest for other land uses”.
items.answer: Deforestation
items.markingKey: Deforestation: the permanent clearing of forest for other land uses. [1]

items.stem: Explain how deforestation can lead to soil erosion.
items.answer: Without a canopy to intercept rain and roots to bind the soil, heavy rain hits bare ground and washes the thin topsoil away; leaching removes nutrients.
items.markingKey: 1 mark no interception/roots; 1 mark rain washes soil [2]

items.stem: Explain how deforestation can reduce rainfall in a region.
items.answer: Fewer trees means less transpiration and evaporation, so less moisture enters the air to form clouds and convectional rain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark less transpiration; 1 mark fewer clouds/rain [2]

items.stem: For deforestation in Borneo, Malaysia and Indonesia or another example of deforestation in a tropical rainforest, briefly describe the impacts of deforestation on people and the environment.
items.answer: deforestation in Borneo, Malaysia and Indonesia: Habitat loss for orangutans, whose numbers have fallen sharply; smoke haze from fires affecting health in Singapore and Malaysia; peat soils releasing large amounts of carbon; land conflicts with local communities; income and jobs from palm oil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Environmental (biodiversity, soils, climate, rivers) and human (indigenous peoples, economy) impacts with figures. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of deforestation in a tropical rainforest (for example deforestation in Borneo, Malaysia and Indonesia). Briefly explain the causes of deforestation.
items.answer: deforestation in Borneo, Malaysia and Indonesia: Clearance for oil palm plantations; commercial logging of hardwoods; forest fires used to clear land; road building and mining.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named economic activities and their scale; government policies; roads opening access. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of deforestation in a tropical rainforest (for example the Amazon rainforest, Brazil). Briefly explain the causes of deforestation.
items.answer: the Amazon rainforest, Brazil: Cattle ranching (about 80% of cleared land), soya farming, commercial logging, mining (e.g. Carajás iron ore), roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway opening the forest to settlers, and hydro-electric dams such as Belo Monte.

items.stem: A student writes: “Desertification is caused only by climate change.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Drought and rising temperatures play a part, but overgrazing, over-cultivation and cutting trees for fuel are major causes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how overgrazing and over-cultivation cause desertification.
items.answer: Too many animals remove vegetation and trample the soil; repeated cropping without fallow exhausts nutrients; bare soil is eroded by wind and rain and becomes infertile.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each process; 1 mark bare soil eroded [3]

items.stem: Explain why population growth in the Sahel has increased desertification.
items.answer: More people need more food and firewood, so more land is grazed and cultivated, trees are cut for fuel and fallow periods are shortened.
items.markingKey: 1 mark more demand; 1 mark land-use effect [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of desertification (for example the Sahel, Africa). Briefly describe the impacts of desertification on people.
items.answer: the Sahel, Africa: Loss of fertile topsoil; falling crop yields and famine (e.g. Niger 2005, 2010); loss of livestock; migration to cities such as Niamey and abroad; conflict over land and water between herders and farmers; dust storms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Food shortages, loss of income, migration, conflict and health impacts. [4]

items.stem: With reference to the Sahel, Africa, or another example of desertification you have studied, explain the causes of desertification.
items.answer: Model answer (the Sahel, Africa): Long droughts since the 1970s and variable rainfall; rapid population growth increasing demand for food and fuelwood; overgrazing by cattle and goats; over-cultivation with shorter fallow periods; cutting trees for firewood.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Physical (drought, rainfall variability) and human (overgrazing, over-cultivation, deforestation, population growth) causes. Levels marking. items.stem: Explain how ecotourism can help protect rainforests.
items.answer: It earns money for local people and governments from keeping the forest intact, provides jobs as guides, funds conservation and educates visitors.
items.markingKey: 1 mark income/jobs; 1 mark incentive to conserve [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.3, information about forest protection in Costa Rica. Forest cover fell to about 21% in the 1980s, then recovered to over half the country by 2020. Farmers receive payments for keeping or replanting forest, and ecotourism lodges employ local guides. Describe the change in forest cover shown.
items.answer: Forest cover rose from 21% in 1985 to over 50% by 2020 – it more than doubled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark trend; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that sustainable management can protect tropical rainforests while still allowing economic development. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: For: Selective logging, agroforestry, ecotourism and payments for ecosystem services (Costa Rica) earn income without destroying the forest. Against: Profits from beef, soya, palm oil and mining are much larger and quicker; enforcement is difficult in remote areas. Population growth and poverty push farmers to clear land. Judgement: It can work where governments enforce laws and international funding rewards protection, but large-scale commercial pressures make it difficult.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2 marks): one simple reason. Level 2 (3-4 marks): one developed reason for AND one against, with an example. [4]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “cutting down only mature trees of certain species and leaving the rest of the forest standing”.

items.markingKey: Selective logging: cutting down only mature trees of certain species and leaving the rest of the forest standing. [1]

items.stem: Fig. 6.3 describes a rainforest area in Costa Rica. In 1985 the forest covered 21% of the country; by 2020 it covered over 50%. About a quarter of the land is in national parks, and tourism earns over US$4 billion a year. (a) Describe the change in forest cover shown. (b) Explain how payments to landowners help protect the forest.
items.answer: (a) Forest cover rose from 21% in 1985 to over 50% by 2020 – it more than doubled. (b) Farmers earn money from keeping trees, so they do not need to clear forest for cattle or crops.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark trend; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark income; 1 mark less clearance [2]

items.stem: Explain what would happen to a food web if a top predator were removed.
items.answer: Its prey (e.g. herbivores) would increase, over-grazing plants and reducing food for other species, which upsets the balance of the whole web.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prey increase; 1 mark knock-on effect [2]

items.answer: In the rainforest plants compete mainly for light, so they grow tall or climb; in the desert they compete mainly for water, so roots are deep or widespread and plants are widely spaced.

Cutting down trees to sell timber for profit.
The gradual change of land in semi-arid areas into desert, caused by drought and human activity.

items.stem: Describe the impacts of deforestation on indigenous peoples.

items.stem: Explain how agroforestry is more sustainable than slash-and-burn farming.
items.answer: Trees remain, so the canopy protects the soil from heavy rain, roots hold soil, and leaf litter keeps adding nutrients, so the land can be farmed for longer.

An arrow from soil labelled “leaching” and an arrow from litter labelled “run-off” are also shown. (a) Name the largest nutrient store. (b) Explain why the transfer from soil to biomass is large.
items.answer: (a) Biomass. (b) Plants grow all year and their dense, shallow roots absorb nutrients as soon as they are released.

items.stem: “The nutrient cycle is the main reason why tropical rainforests are fragile ecosystems.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Most nutrients are held in the biomass; once trees are removed, heavy rain leaches the thin soil and fertility collapses within a few years. Against: Interdependence in food webs means removing one species affects many others; the forest also depends on recycling its own rainfall through transpiration. Climate change and fire threaten even untouched forest. Judgement: The nutrient cycle is a key reason, because clearing breaks it so quickly, but interdependence and the water cycle add to the fragility.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the loss of water vapour from plants through tiny pores (stomata) in their leaves”.
items.answer: Transpiration
items.markingKey: Transpiration: the loss of water vapour from plants through tiny pores (stomata) in their leaves. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain two ways in which desert plants reduce water loss. (b) A student writes: “Rainforest trees have deep roots to reach groundwater.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Small or no leaves (spines) reduce surface area for transpiration; thick waxy cuticle; stomata that open only at night; hairs that trap moist air. (b) Not correct. Most nutrients are near the surface, so roots are shallow; buttress roots give support.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks each developed adaptation [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 6.2 shows the area of forest (km²) in a state in the Brazilian Amazon: 2000: 150 000, 2003: 148 500, 2006: 146 500, 2009: 145 000, 2012: 143 000. Calculate the percentage of the 2000 forest lost by 2012.

Study Fig. 6.4. Plant X: a tall tree with buttress roots, drip-tip leaves and thin bark. Plant Y: a cactus with a swollen stem, a waxy coating, spines and a wide, shallow root system. (a) State which plant grows in a tropical rainforest and which in a hot desert. (b) Explain how two features help plant X to survive.
items.answer: (a) X: tropical rainforest. Y: hot desert. (b) Buttress roots support the tall tree in shallow soil; drip tips shed heavy rain to stop rot; thin bark because no protection from cold is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 2 marks each developed adaptation [4]

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.4. Plant X: a tall tree with buttress roots, drip-tip leaves and thin bark. Plant Y: a cactus with a swollen stem, a waxy coating, spines and a wide, shallow root system. (a) State which plant grows in a tropical rainforest and which in a hot desert. (b) Explain how two features help plant X to survive. (c) Suggest why plant Y’s roots spread so widely near the surface.
items.answer: (a) X: tropical rainforest. Y: hot desert. (b) Buttress roots support the tall tree in shallow soil; drip tips shed heavy rain to stop rot; thin bark because no protection from cold is needed. (c) Rain is rare and does not soak deeply, so roots must collect water from a large area quickly before it evaporates.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 2 marks each developed adaptation [4] (c) 1 mark rare rain; 1 mark quick absorption [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “desertification”?
options: Large-scale commercial farming of beef cattle on pasture, the main cause of Amazon deforestation.
Cutting down trees to sell timber for profit.
The gradual change of land in semi-arid areas into desert, caused by drought and human activity.
Growing food mainly to feed the farmer’s own family.
items.answer: The gradual change of land in semi-arid areas into desert, caused by drought and human activity.
items.markingKey: Desertification: the gradual change of land in semi-arid areas into desert, caused by drought and human activity. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Rainforest soils remain fertile for many decades after clearing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Without the nutrient cycle they become infertile within a few years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Desertification is caused only by climate change.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how deforestation can lead to soil erosion.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Drought and rising temperatures play a part, but overgrazing, over-cultivation and cutting trees for fuel are major causes. (b) Without a canopy to intercept rain and roots to bind the soil, heavy rain hits bare ground and washes the thin topsoil away; leaching removes nutrients.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark no interception/roots; 1 mark rain washes soil [2]

items.stem: Fig. 6.2 shows the area of forest (km²) in a province of Borneo: 2000: 120 000, 2003: 116 500, 2006: 115 500, 2009: 114 000, 2012: 109 500. Calculate the percentage of the 2000 forest lost by 2012.
Name one example of deforestation in a tropical rainforest you have studied and, for that example, explain the causes of deforestation.
items.answer: the Amazon rainforest, Brazil: Cattle ranching (about 80% of cleared land), soya farming, commercial logging, mining (e.g. Carajás iron ore), roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway opening the forest to settlers, and hydro-electric dams such as Belo Monte.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named economic activities and their scale; government policies; roads opening access. [4]

items.stem: Using a case study of deforestation in a tropical rainforest, such as the Amazon rainforest, Brazil, explain the causes of deforestation.
items.answer: Model answer (the Amazon rainforest, Brazil): Cattle ranching (about 80% of cleared land), soya farming, commercial logging, mining (e.g. Carajás iron ore), roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway opening the forest to settlers, and hydro-electric dams such as Belo Monte.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Named economic activities and their scale; government policies; roads opening access. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Fig. 6.2 shows the area of forest (km²) in a state in the Brazilian Amazon: 2005: 150 000, 2008: 148 500, 2011: 147 000, 2014: 145 500, 2017: 141 000. (a) Identify the period with the greatest loss. (b) Suggest two reasons for the loss of forest. (c) Explain two environmental impacts of the loss shown.
items.answer: (a) 2014-2017 (4500 km²) (b) Clearing for cattle ranching or plantations (soya, oil palm); logging; mining; road building and new settlements; HEP reservoirs. (c) Loss of habitat and biodiversity; soil erosion and leaching; less transpiration so less rainfall; carbon released, adding to climate change.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 2 marks each developed impact [4]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Stone lines (bunds) help water soak into the soil in the Sahel.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They slow run-off so water infiltrates and soil is trapped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why international cooperation is needed to protect rainforests.
items.answer: Demand for beef, soya, palm oil and timber comes from other countries; forests store carbon and biodiversity for the whole world; poorer countries need funding (e.g. debt-for-nature swaps, REDD+).
items.markingKey: 1 mark global demand; 1 mark global benefit/funding [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.3, information about forest protection in Costa Rica. Forest cover fell to about 21% in the 1980s, then recovered to over half the country by 2020. Farmers receive payments for keeping or replanting forest, and ecotourism lodges employ local guides. Explain how ecotourism benefits local people and the environment.
items.answer: Jobs as guides and in lodges, income kept locally; money and incentive to protect wildlife and forest; small numbers of visitors cause little damage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark people; 1 mark environment [2]
